title: Carbon Monoxide: Please Just Listen Anyway
summary: Stuff You Should Know PSA-edition episode on carbon monoxide. The hosts explain why CO is deadly (it binds hemoglobin far more readily than oxygen), how it forms from incomplete combustion, and its history from the thirteenth-century alchemist Arnaldus de Villa Nova through Helmont and Joseph Priestley. They cover acute and chronic poisoning, sources in homes (unvented space heaters, cars left running in attached garages, generators, incense, hookahs, cigarettes, gas appliances), the 2021 Texas winter storm grill deaths, outdoor and urban CO, Fairbanks temperature inversions, NASA's MOPITT satellite, the catalytic converter, detector advice, and medical uses of CO. The episode also includes a listener mail segment and a few ad/promotional reads.
topics: carbon monoxide and methane hydroxyl radicals

segments.summary: Josh and an announcer promote upcoming live shows in Washington D.C., Greater Boston, and Toronto, with ticket info.

segments.title: Opening banter and PSA framing
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the PSA-edition episode, recall past PSAs and the cellophane bags short stuff, and note the serious topic of carbon monoxide.

segments.title: What carbon monoxide is and how it forms
segments.summary: CO is a deadly gas that is produced by combustion, especially incomplete combustion. It has no smell or warning. Perfect (stoichiometric) combustion is theoretical, and inefficiencies from air-fuel mix or cooling produce CO.

segments.title: History of CO discovery
segments.summary: Arnaldus de Villa Nova in the thirteenth century noted poisonous gas from burning wood; Helmont in 1644 described gas carbonum; Joseph Priestley in the 1770s identified air components and called CO heavy inflammable air.

segments.title: Word origin tangent: inflammable
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how inflammable came to be replaced by flammable because the word confused people.

segments.title: Hosts' banter and the Jerry joke
segments.summary: Light banter about the hosts poking fun at each other and at Jerry, and a belly joke.

segments.title: How CO kills: hemoglobin binding
segments.summary: CO binds hemoglobin about 210 times more readily than oxygen, displacing oxygen, causing hypoxia. Exposure levels and equilibrium percentages are discussed.

segments.title: Symptoms, acute and chronic poisoning
segments.summary: Discussion of ppm levels, symptoms like headache, nausea, dizziness, carboxyhemoglobin persisting around four hours, relapse risk, and chronic poisoning at low levels over time.
topics: acute vs chronic carbon monoxide poisoning

segments.title: Banter on prank calls and the Jerky Boys
segments.summary: Hosts joke about prank calls and the Jerky Boys cassette and possible future episodes.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break.

segments.title: Smoking, hookahs, incense and fire deaths
segments.summary: Smoke inhalation in fires and CO's role; cigarette smokers' carboxyhemoglobin levels; hookah and incense exposure; hosts share personal incense experiences.

segments.title: CO death and injury statistics
segments.summary: Around 400 Americans die yearly from accidental CO poisoning, about 100,000 go to the ER and 14,000 are hospitalized overnight; vulnerable groups are more at risk.

segments.title: Unvented space heaters and home sources
segments.summary: Unvented kerosene and natural gas space heaters are a major hazard; CPSC lists them among dangerous household products. Hosts recall wall-recessed heaters called chill chasers.

segments.title: Oxygen sensors on heaters and car left running in garage
segments.summary: Newer heaters have oxygen sensors that shut them off. Josh describes accidentally leaving a hybrid running in an attached garage. Banter about hybrid car-on/car-off voice prompts.

segments.title: Texas 2021 winter storm and global household air pollution
segments.summary: Grills and charcoal used indoors during the 2021 Texas freeze killed eleven people and sent about 1,400 to the ER; Texas rejected requiring detectors. Open fires worldwide and WHO estimate of household air pollution deaths in 2020 are discussed.

segments.title: Portable indoor ventilation hood invention
segments.summary: Hosts recall a Carnegie Mellon student invention of a cheap portable ventilation hood for indoor cooking from about 2008.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break.

segments.title: Generators and Fairbanks inversion
segments.summary: Portable generators placed near homes after disasters can kill; keep at least twenty feet away. Fairbanks, Alaska's temperature inversion traps pollution and CO.

segments.title: NASA MOPITT satellite and CO trends
segments.summary: NASA's Terra satellite with MOPITT sensor measures CO from high altitude; CO concentrations declined since 2000. Satellites also help check national emissions claims.

segments.title: Clean Air Act and CO's effect on methane and climate
segments.summary: The 1970 Clean Air Act helped reduce pollution. CO reacts with hydroxyl radicals, leaving methane to accumulate and indirectly affecting climate change.

segments.title: Catalytic converters
segments.summary: Eugene Houdry's catalytic converter, combined with removal of leaded gas in the mid-1970s, reduced CO. Converters use platinum, palladium, and rhodium to convert CO to CO2. Thefts of converters are mentioned.

segments.title: Home prevention: furnaces, appliances, tune-ups
segments.summary: Keep furnace filters clean, keep exhaust fans working, consider induction cooktops, have gas cooktops tuned up with combustion testing, and clean burner parts.

segments.title: Carbon monoxide detectors
segments.summary: Use CO detectors; newer smoke detectors may combine functions. Plug-in detectors with battery backup are inexpensive. CO mixes with air evenly, so placement high or low does not matter much.

segments.title: Beneficial and medical uses of CO
segments.summary: Mention of CO used to keep meat red (deferred as a possible future short stuff) and its medical use at higher concentrations to treat acute respiratory distress syndrome.
